The suspension did not instantly deprive the army of its existing equipment, however, and should not be treated as the direct military cause of defeat. Its greater importance was political: repression and instability had made continued support increasingly costly for Washington. This fits a revisionist interpretation in which Batista’s internal weaknesses helped alter the international circumstances surrounding the struggle (Pérez, 1988). Castro also benefited from opportunities abroad that his movement actively cultivated. Exile in Mexico allowed him to organize and train followers before the *Granma* departed from Tuxpan on 25 November 1956. Nevertheless, Mexican territory as an organizing base should be distinguished from official Mexican sponsorship; the authorities arrested Castro and other revolutionaries in June 1956. More direct assistance became available from Venezuela after the overthrow of Marcos Pérez Jiménez on 23 January 1958. Under the provisional leadership of Wolfgang Larrazábal, Venezuela became a source of arms and support for the Cuban insurgency during 1958 (Quirk, 1993). These developments show that foreign assistance strengthened the rebels, but do not establish that outside powers determined the outcome. Soviet support, in particular, does not explain the January 1959 victory. External aid and diplomatic distancing were contributing factors whose effectiveness depended on developments inside Cuba. Batista’s weaknesses were therefore a catalyst to a substantial extent: they damaged his international standing while making assistance to his opponents appear increasingly practical and politically defensible.\n\nUnited opposition made Batista’s weaknesses more consequential by connecting groups that differed over Cuba’s future but agreed that his government must end. Castro’s guerrillas alone could not represent every constituency opposed to the dictatorship. Students, urban militants, sections of organized labor, middle-class professionals, and established political opponents contributed distinct networks and resources. Sweig’s *Inside the Cuban Revolution* (2002) supports a revisionist interpretation by demonstrating the importance of the urban underground alongside the Sierra Maestra leadership. Frank País’s organization in Santiago, for example, coordinated the uprising of 30 November 1956 to support the anticipated arrival of the *Granma* expedition. Although the landing occurred later than expected, the episode demonstrates that revolutionary strategy extended beyond guerrilla warfare. Cooperation also required a political program capable of attracting people who did not share identical ideological commitments. The Sierra Maestra Manifesto of 12 July 1957, associated with Castro, Raúl Chibás, and Felipe Pazos, advocated a provisional civilian government and elections, helping present the rebellion as a broader constitutional alternative. The Caracas Pact of 20 July 1958 subsequently brought major opposition organizations into an agreement against Batista. Nevertheless, “united opposition” should describe an evolving coalition rather than complete harmony. The failed strike of 9 April 1958 revealed weaknesses in coordination and mobilization, while revolutionary organizations continued to disagree over leadership and tactics. Batista’s continued rule nevertheless supplied a common objective strong enough to sustain cooperation. After his flight on 1 January 1959, Castro’s call for a general strike helped frustrate attempts to establish a military successor, demonstrating the importance of civilian mobilization alongside battlefield victories. Thus, unity substantially contributed to victory, but its foundations were partly negative: rejection of the dictatorship preceded agreement on the revolution’s eventual direction.
